title: Interference & Resonance
hook: When waves overlap they add up — in step they reinforce, out of step they cancel. Drive a system at its natural beat and it swings ever bigger: resonance.
key_points: Overlapping waves combine: in phase they reinforce (constructive), out of phase they cancel (destructive).
Destructive interference is how noise-canceling headphones quiet sound.
Trapped waves settle into standing-wave patterns — the basis of musical notes.
Driving a system at its natural frequency builds large oscillations — resonance, like a pushed swing.
content_html: Waves don't bounce off each other when they meet — they pass through and simply add up. Where two crests line up the wave grows taller (constructive interference); where a crest meets a trough they flatten out (destructive interference). That cancellation isn't just a curiosity: noise-canceling headphones listen to the sound around you and play back an opposite wave that flattens it to near silence.
extra_html: Confine a wave — on a guitar string or in a pipe — and it interferes with its own reflections to form a steady standing-wave pattern, which is what gives an instrument its distinct notes. Push a system at the exact rhythm it likes to vibrate, its natural frequency, and each push adds to the last until the motion grows large. That's resonance, the same reason a well-timed shove sends a swing higher and higher. Wikipedia's article on wave interference covers how waves combine and the standing-wave and resonance behavior that follows.

flashcards.prompt: What's the difference between constructive and destructive interference?
flashcards.back_html: When waves overlap in step their crests add up and reinforce (constructive); when they overlap out of step crests meet troughs and cancel (destructive).

choices.text: They emit a wave that destructively interferes with the noise, canceling it
They physically block all sound with thick padding
They speed up the incoming sound waves until you can't hear them

flashcards.explanation_html: The headphones produce an anti-noise wave that's out of step with the incoming sound, so the two cancel through destructive interference.

choices.text: Driving a system at its natural frequency so its oscillations grow large
Two waves passing through each other unchanged
A wave losing all its energy to friction

flashcards.explanation_html: Push a system at the rhythm it naturally wants to vibrate at and the energy builds up, producing big oscillations — just like timing pushes on a swing.
